idiom_name: defer release() at the acquisition site; Close/Release methods that hand the resource back (database/sql convention)
implementation_notes: Go has no destructors, so the hand-back is a documented method plus defer: write defer r.Release() (or defer rows.Close()) on the line after a successful checkout and the release runs on every return path, panics included. This defer-and-convention idiom is what replaces the smart-pointer structure; ownership lives in the documentation and in the method name, not in the type. The standard library shows the convention to copy: database/sql's Conn.Close 'returns the connection to the connection pool' rather than closing the socket, and Rows.Close releases the connection the same way - so a package that lends resources should expose a Release/Close whose doc comment says it returns the resource to its owner, and keep any real destroy path unexported. A wrapper struct carrying the release is justified only when many call sites must be protected uniformly; Go's idiom stays defer.
pitfalls: defer inside a loop accumulates until the surrounding function returns, holding borrowed resources long past their use; extract the body into a function or release explicitly inside the loop.
A deferred call evaluates its receiver immediately but runs later, so a variable reassigned by a retry loop hands back the wrong instance - defer the release right after each successful acquisition.
A typed-nil or an interface value wrapping a nil pointer passes an err != nil check only by luck; calling Release on it can panic or silently return a zero resource to the pool.
runtime.SetFinalizer is not a hand-back: it runs on GC scheduling, so it is at best a bug detector, never the release mechanism.
